question: When viewed as matrices, which flags of African nations have the same linear algebraic rank as the flag of Denmark? Assume that values in each matrix are chosen so that the rank of each flag is maximal.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I would choose **Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau**.

Denmark’s flag has maximal rank **2**: after collapsing repeated rows/columns in its color-block matrix, the red field with a white Nordic cross has two independent row/column directions. The African flags with the same block-rank are those whose color pattern reduces to a single vertical hoist stripe plus a two-band fly, giving a 2-by-2 block structure. Benin and Madagascar clearly have this form. Guinea-Bissau also has the same underlying rank-2 block pattern: the red vertical stripe with yellow/green horizontal bands determines the row and column spaces, and the centered black star does not introduce a new independent row/column mode when values are chosen for maximal rank. So I would include Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I would model each flag by its minimal rectangular color-block matrix and take the maximal rank over choices of distinct color values. Denmark gives a 3×3 pattern essentially  
\[
\begin{matrix}
r&w&r\\
w&w&w\\
r&w&r
\end{matrix}
\]
which has rank 2. Benin and Madagascar both reduce to a 2×2 block pattern such as  
\[
\begin{matrix}
g&y\\
g&r
\end{matrix}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\begin{matrix}
w&r\\
w&g
\end{matrix}
\]
so they also have maximal rank 2. Guinea-Bissau has the same coarse block structure as Benin/Madagascar: a full-height vertical stripe on the hoist and two horizontal regions on the fly. The black star lies inside the vertical stripe as a local motif, so it does not create a new independent row/column direction at the coarse matrix level. Therefore I would select Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I get Denmark as rank 2: its two-color cross matrix can be written as \(J - ab^T\), where \(J\) is the all-ones matrix and \(a,b\) are nonconstant row/column indicators, so it has exactly two independent directions. Among African flags, the rank-2 cases are Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau. Benin and Madagascar have the same hoist-stripe/fly-split structure—a vertical stripe on the hoist and two horizontal blocks on the fly—giving a 2-by-2 block pattern with three colors and maximal rank 2. Guinea-Bissau has the same underlying stripe/split matrix; its black star lies inside the hoist stripe, so under the maximal-rank assignment it adds only a row-dependent perturbation within that already-present stripe and does not introduce a third independent column direction. Thus it also has rank 2.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The flags are Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau. Denmark has maximal rank 2: its Nordic cross gives exactly two independent column types—columns through the white vertical stripe, and columns outside it with a white horizontal band on a red field. Benin and Madagascar have the same structure: a full-height hoist stripe plus two horizontal fly bands, yielding two independent column types. Guinea-Bissau also has this structure—a red hoist stripe with yellow/green fly bands. Its black star lies entirely within the red hoist stripe and does not create a new independent column direction beyond the red hoist and yellow/green fly columns, so its maximal rank is also 2. Thus these three African flags match Denmark’s rank.

Denmark’s flag has maximal matrix rank 2: the red background gives one constant direction, while the white cross is generated by a vertical stripe factor and a horizontal stripe factor, so the whole pattern is a sum of two independent rank-one pieces. The African flags with the same rank-2 structure are Benin and Guinea-Bissau. Both have a full-height vertical band at the hoist and a horizontal two-color split in the remaining fly-side rectangle. In matrix terms, their columns reduce to two basic types: the hoist-band columns and the fly columns that are constant on the top and bottom horizontal regions. This gives a column space spanned by two independent directions, so the maximal rank is 2. Guinea-Bissau’s black star is confined within the hoist band, so it is an internal marking inside an already-existing band and does not introduce a new independent row/column direction beyond that rank-2 decomposition.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The flags are Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau. Denmark’s flag has maximal rank 2: its pattern reduces to two independent row types and two independent column types. Benin and Madagascar have the same two-type decomposition—a full-height vertical hoist band together with a two-band horizontal split on the fly. Guinea-Bissau has the identical geometric structure (red hoist band plus yellow/green upper and lower fly bands); its black star is confined to the hoist band and does not introduce an extra independent row/column direction, so under maximal-choice values its rank also stays at 2. 10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Benin and Madagascar.

The flag of Denmark has maximal matrix rank \(2\): its color pattern reduces to row types like \([R,W,R]\) and \([W,W,W]\), so at most two independent rows/columns are possible, and suitable distinct numerical values for red and white achieve rank \(2\).

Among African national flags, the ones with the same maximal rank \(2\) are:

- **Benin**: green vertical hoist band, with yellow over red on the fly. This is essentially a \(2\times2\) color pattern, e.g. \(\begin{pmatrix}G&Y\\G&R\end{pmatrix}\), which can have rank \(2\).
- **Madagascar**: white vertical hoist band, with red over green on the fly. Similarly, \(\begin{pmatrix}W&R\\W&G\end{pmatrix}\) can have rank \(2\).

Other African flags are either rank \(1\) (plain horizontal/vertical stripes) or rank greater than \(2\) due to diagonals, triangles, stars, crescents, or emblems.

Thus I would exclude Guinea-Bissau unless the intended model deliberately ignores emblems or uses very coarse blocks.

Simple horizontal/vertical stripe flags are rank 1. Flags with diagonals, triangles, stars, crescents, or other emblems generally have rank ≥3.

Current best answer: **Benin and Madagascar**. Unresolved issue: exact modeling convention for emblems/small details; if emblems are ignored, Guinea-Bissau could also qualify, but the “maximal rank” phrasing suggests they should count.

Once the star is counted, it forces extra row/column variation inside the hoist stripe; the usual witness submatrix has determinant \(R(R-B)(G-Y)\), generically nonzero, so Guinea-Bissau’s maximal rank is at least \(3\), not \(2\).

The block-convention argument is not stable. If we allow coarse-graining that ignores/collapses emblems, then other flags join as well. For example, even with São Tomé’s triangular red hoist, its base pattern without stars can already be rank \(2\):
\[

\[
\begin{pmatrix}G&Y\\ G&R\end{pmatrix},

with no non-rectangular emblem adding an independent direction. Their maximal rank is exactly \(2\), matching Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau’s black star is a genuine non-rectangular color region inside the red hoist stripe. Under a faithful color-region matrix, it introduces extra row and column types. The standard witness still applies: take rows above the star, through the star, and below the star, and columns through red hoist away from the star, through the star, and in the fly. \[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&R&Y\\
B&R&Y\\
B&R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
has determinant \(R(R-B)(G-Y)\), generically nonzero. So Guinea-Bissau’s maximal rank is at least \(3\), not \(2\). This is not arbitrary pixelation; it only uses the actual presence of a distinct star region.

\[

\begin{pmatrix}W&R\\ W&G\end{pmatrix},

with no non-rectangular emblem forcing extra independent row/column behavior. Their maximal rank is exactly \(2\), matching Denmark.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the discussion has narrowed to the right issue: the determinant witness for Guinea-Bissau is valid only after we choose a refined raster around the star. I agree it is a real calculation, but I don’t think it settles the intended matrix model.

The problem says values in each matrix are chosen so the rank is maximal. That prevents us from accidentally collapsing distinct entries of a given matrix. It does **not** say we are free to choose the row/column partition so as to increase rank. For Denmark, the natural matrix is not a pixel bitmap; it is the stripe-factor matrix. Its rank 2 comes from a full-height vertical arm and a full-width horizontal arm. Under that same block-level convention, Guinea-Bissau has a full-height red hoist factor and a yellow/green fly factor, giving the block matrix  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&Y\\
R&G
\end{pmatrix},
\]
which generically has rank 2. The black star is a charge inside the already-existing red hoist field. It changes values within that hoist block, but it does not create a new full-height or full-width stripe direction.

C3 and C4, I understand why the determinant submatrix pushed you toward exclusion, but I think it changes the matrix model only for Guinea-Bissau. If we subdivide around the star, the answer becomes dependent on star size, curvature, and raster resolution, none of which the problem specifies. Denmark’s cross is axis-aligned, but that is a property of its shape, not a rule that curved charges must be rasterized. The “maximal rank” clause prevents collapsing distinct entries of the chosen matrix; it does not require refining the chosen matrix until an emblem adds rank.

São Tomé is not a clean counterexample because its red hoist element is a triangle whose width changes row by row, so it does not reduce to a single full-height hoist stripe even before the stars. That is different from Guinea-Bissau’s star lying inside an already-existing red hoist rectangle.

So under the coherent block-level convention that makes Denmark rank 2, the best set remains **Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau**. Excluding Guinea-Bissau requires explicitly adopting a finer, resolution-dependent convention for its star, and I still don’t see a principled statement of why that convention should apply only there.
